title: Writing and influence for security work
summary: Write findings, reports, executive summaries, risk memos, incident updates, review comments, board briefings and disclosures that get read and acted on, through Equifax, Storm-0558 and Project Zero.
outcomes: Write a finding whose title, impact, evidence and fix let an owner act without asking you a question
State severity with its scale, environment adjustments and confidence, using CVSS nomenclature correctly
Write executive summaries, risk memos and exceptions that end in a decision by a named risk owner
Write incident updates that separate confirmed facts, calibrated judgements and unknowns, and correct errors
Write review comments and fix requests that get security changes shipped without formal authority
Brief a board with business risks, measures of control and clear asks, and write vendor reports and advisories

lessons.title: Writing is a security control: Equifax's patch email

blocks.md:
Most security work ends in writing. A tester's finding, an analyst's escalation, an engineer's review comment: each one only matters if a reader understands it and does something. When the words fail, the control fails, even if the technical work was perfect.

Tiny example. Two messages report the same bug:

1. "FYI, there is a critical Struts vulnerability, please patch as appropriate."
2. "Priya: the dispute portal runs Struts 2.3.31, which attackers are exploiting now. Please patch it by Thursday 17:00; reply here when done or if you are blocked."

The first informs everyone and obliges no one. The second names a reader, a system, a reason, an action, a deadline and a way to report back.

That gap is not hypothetical. In March 2017 the Apache Struts project disclosed CVE-2017-5638, a flaw in a widely used Java web framework (recall the Equifax case from security-basics). The US House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform investigated the Equifax breach that followed and published its majority staff report in December 2018. It describes how the warning travelled inside Equifax:

- 7 March: Struts discloses the flaw and releases the patch.
- 8 March: US-CERT (the US Computer Emergency Readiness Team, the government's alerting centre) emails Equifax.
- 9 March: Equifax's GTVM team (Global Threat and Vulnerability Management) forwards the alert to a mailing list, asking anyone running Struts to patch within 48 hours. The report counts 430 recipients.
- 10 March: first evidence of attackers exploiting the flaw on Equifax servers, one day after the email.
- 15 March: a scan finds no vulnerable internet-facing system.
- 13 May: attackers break in through the unpatched dispute portal and stay for 76 days.

blocks.title: How the Struts warning travelled inside Equifax (2017)

scenes.caption: 8 March: US-CERT alerts Equifax's vulnerability team. The information is correct and arrives a day after disclosure.
9 March: GTVM emails a list of about 430 people. It tells whoever is responsible for Struts installations to patch within 48 hours, without naming anyone.
The policy named roles (business, system and application owner) but, witnesses testified, nobody was officially designated for them. No one on the list was clearly obliged to act.
15 March: a scan of external systems finds nothing, so the silence looks like success. Struts had been spotted in ACIS in January 2017, but nobody documented or tracked it.
13 May: attackers exploit the unpatched portal. The report finds no redundancy: no follow-up message checked that the right person had acted.

blocks.md:
Equifax fired Graeme Payne, a senior vice president whose area included ACIS (the Automated Consumer Interview System, the dispute portal), for, as human resources told them, failing to forward an email. The committee report records Payne's answer: they were one of 430 recipients, copied for information, and not a system or application owner under the policy. The former CEO, Richard Smith, told Congress the cause was "human error"; Payne called that "a gross simplification".

The writing lesson is not about who was to blame. A broadcast to 430 people is a message with no addressee. Security writing works when it answers four questions for one specific reader: **who** must act, **what** exactly, **by when**, and **how** they will tell you it is done.

blocks.code:
To: Dispute Portal owners (ACIS): Ana Ruiz (app), Sam Lee (servers)
Cc: GTVM, CIO Global Platforms
Subject: ACTION by Sat 11 Mar 09:30 - patch Apache Struts on ACIS (CVE-2017-5638)

ACIS uses Apache Struts 2. CVE-2017-5638 lets an unauthenticated
attacker run commands on the server; attacks are already happening.

Please:
  1. Apply Struts 2.3.32 (or 2.5.10.1) to every ACIS server.
  2. Reply "done" with the version string, or "blocked" with the reason.

If we have no reply by Sat 09:30, GTVM will call you and then escalate
to the CIO. GTVM will rescan within 48 hours of your reply to confirm.
Not running Struts? Reply "not affected" so we can close the item.
blocks.caption: An illustrative rewrite, not a real Equifax message. The names are invented; the fixed Struts versions are the ones in the Apache S2-045 bulletin. It names owners, a deadline, three replies, a follow-up and a check. CIO is the chief information officer, the executive in charge of IT.

blocks.md: A security message is a control with a single point of failure: the reader. Write it to one accountable person, say what to do and by when, and say what happens if they do not answer.

blocks.question: Under Equifax's 2016 patch policy, why was a 430-person email a weak control even though its content was correct?
options: The email was sent too late to matter
Nobody was officially designated as owner, so no recipient was clearly obliged to act, and nothing checked for a reply
US-CERT alerts are not trustworthy enough to act on
Emails cannot contain patch instructions
blocks.explain: The alert went out two days after disclosure, well before the May intrusion. The failure was ownership and follow-up: roles existed on paper without designees, and the report found no redundancy to confirm the right person had acted.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite exercise. Take this broadcast and rewrite it for one accountable reader: "All teams: a critical OpenSSL issue was announced today. Please update as appropriate." What must your version contain?
blocks.reveal:
A strong rewrite names:

- **The reader**: the owner of the specific systems, by name or team (find them in your asset inventory, not in a mailing list).
- **What and where**: which hosts run the affected version and how you know (scan date, package inventory).
- **Why now**: impact in one sentence, and whether exploitation is known.
- **The action**: the fixed version or the mitigation.
- **The deadline** and the **reply you want** ("done" with version, "blocked" with reason, or "not affected").
- **Follow-up**: when you will check, how you will verify, and who you escalate to if there is no answer.

lessons.title: Plain, direct and first: sentences a busy reader acts on

blocks.md:
**Plain language** means writing your reader can understand and use the first time they read it. The US government's plain language guidance (now kept by Digital.gov, the General Services Administration's site for digital teams) states the first rule as: write for your audience. That does not mean dumbing down. A detection engineer and a chief financial officer need different words for the same fact.

Tiny example, same fact twice:

- "It was observed that various systems may potentially be affected and it is recommended that appropriate patches be applied as needed."
- "Two internet-facing servers run a Struts version that attackers are exploiting now. The ACIS team should patch both by Friday."

The second is shorter, but that is not the point. It says what, where, how bad, who and when.

Four habits from the guidance do most of the work:

- **Active voice.** The guidance's own example: not "It must be done," but "You must do it." Passive voice ("patches should be applied") hides who acts, which in security writing is the most important fact.
- **Present tense** where you can: "the server accepts the old password" is stronger than "it was found that the server would accept".
- **No hidden verbs.** A hidden verb is a verb turned into a noun: "perform an analysis of" instead of "analyse", "make a recommendation" instead of "recommend".
- **Organise for the reader.** Summarise long documents up front, use lists and tables. Many teams call this **BLUF**, bottom line up front: the conclusion and the ask come first, the reasoning after.

blocks.code:
import re

VAGUE = ["may", "might", "potentially", "various", "appropriate", "as needed"]
PASSIVE = re.compile(r"\b(is|are|was|were|be|been)\s+(\w+ed)\b", re.I)

def check(text):
    words = len(text.split())
    vague = [w for w in VAGUE if re.search(r"\b" + w + r"\b", text, re.I)]
    passive = [" ".join(m) for m in PASSIVE.findall(text)]
    print(f"{words} words | vague: {vague} | passive: {passive}")

before = ("It was observed that various systems may potentially be affected "
          "and it is recommended that appropriate patches be applied as needed.")
after = ("Two internet-facing servers run a Struts version that attackers "
         "are exploiting now. The ACIS team should patch both by Friday.")
check(before)
check(after)
blocks.caption: A rough checker, run for real (Python 3). It flags a few vague words and the simple pattern 'to be' plus a word ending in -ed. It is a heuristic: it misses irregular passives such as 'was found' and can flag harmless phrases. Use it to start a revision, not to grade one.

blocks.code:
21 words | vague: ['may', 'potentially', 'various', 'appropriate', 'as needed'] | passive: ['was observed', 'be affected', 'is recommended', 'be applied']
20 words | vague: [] | passive: []
blocks.caption: Real output. Almost the same length, yet the first sentence names no system, no actor and no deadline.

blocks.title: Same fact, two drafts: what the checker counts

scenes.caption: The vague draft: 21 words, five hedges and four passive phrases. A reader cannot tell what is affected or who should act.
The rewrite: 20 words, no hedges, no passives, and it carries four facts the reader needs (systems, threat, owner, deadline). Length barely changed; content did.

blocks.md: Hedging is not the same as honesty. "May potentially" hides uncertainty instead of stating it. If you are unsure, say what you know, what you do not, and how sure you are (the incident lesson later in this course gives you the words). If you are sure, do not hedge to sound modest.

Two more habits matter in security writing specifically:

- **Define or drop jargon.** "SSRF to IMDS" (server-side request forgery against the cloud instance metadata service) means something to a cloud security engineer and nothing to a product manager. For mixed audiences write the effect ("the server can be tricked into fetching its own cloud credentials") and put the term in brackets.
- **One idea per sentence, numbers instead of adjectives.** "Many hosts" invites argument; "17 of 52 hosts" invites action. "Critical" is a label; "lets anyone on the internet read every customer's address" is a reason.

blocks.question: Which sentence follows the plain language guidance best for a message to a service owner?
options: Your login service accepts expired session tokens; please deploy the fix in pull request 812 by Wednesday.
It is recommended that remediation of the identified issue be performed in a timely manner.
Remediation should be considered by the relevant stakeholders.
A potential weakness may exist in some authentication components.
blocks.explain: It is active, present tense, names the system, the defect, the action and the deadline. The others are passive, use hidden verbs ('remediation be performed') and leave out who and when.

blocks.question: Why is passive voice especially harmful in a security recommendation?
options: It is grammatically wrong
It makes sentences too short
It hides who must act, and ownership is usually the thing that decides whether a fix happens
Executives do not understand passive voice
blocks.explain: Plain language guidance notes that passive voice obscures who handles what. In remediation, an action with no named actor is the Equifax failure in miniature.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite exercise. "Following the completion of the assessment, it was determined that there is a lack of enforcement of multi-factor authentication on a number of administrative accounts, which could potentially result in compromise." Rewrite it in two sentences.
blocks.reveal:
One good version:

"12 of 40 administrator accounts in the identity provider can sign in with a password alone. A phished or reused password for any of them gives full admin access; the IAM (identity and access management) team should require MFA for the admin group by 30 November."

What changed: a number replaced "a number of", "lack of enforcement" became the verb phrase "can sign in with a password alone", the vague "could potentially result in compromise" became a concrete consequence, and an owner and date were added. (MFA, multi-factor authentication, needs no expansion for this audience; for a board it would.)

lessons.title: Writing a finding: title, impact, evidence, fix

blocks.md:
A **finding** is one documented security problem: what is wrong, why it matters, how you know, and how to fix it. You met its fields in pentest-methodology-recon ("Reporting: from finding to fix, and the retest"). This lesson is about writing each field well, because each one is read by a different person for a different decision.

Tiny example. A weak finding title: "XSS vulnerability". A strong one: "Stored XSS in support-ticket subject runs in agents' sessions". (XSS, cross-site scripting, recalled from web-security-model: script supplied by one party runs in another user's page.) The second tells a triager what kind of bug, where it lives and who it hurts, before they open the finding.

**The title** is the most-read line. It appears in ticket lists, dashboards and the executive summary table. A reliable shape is *weakness + location + consequence*: "Missing ownership check on /api/invoices/{id} exposes all customers' invoices". Avoid tool names ("Burp found..."), CVE numbers alone, and words like "issue" or "problem".

**The impact** answers "so what?" for this client, not for the internet in general. Write it as a scenario: who the attacker is (anyone on the internet, a logged-in customer, an employee), what they do, and what the organisation loses. NIST's guidance on risk registers (NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1) suggests the same cause-and-effect shape for risk descriptions: if this event happens, then this harm follows. Name data and numbers: "any customer can read any other customer's invoices (about 48,000 accounts)" beats "data exposure".

**The evidence** convinces a sceptical engineer that the finding is real and lets them reproduce the check. Give the exact request or configuration, the observed response, the time (UTC) and the account you used. Redact secrets and personal data in the report itself: show the first and last characters of a token, blur names, never paste a full session cookie. Evidence is not a story of your afternoon; keep only what proves the claim.

**The fix** must be specific enough to act on and ordered by urgency: what to do today (contain), what to change in code or configuration (correct), and what would stop the whole class of bug (prevent). "Implement input validation" is not a fix. "Encode the subject field with the template engine's HTML escaping on output; add a strict Content Security Policy as a second layer" is. Every finding also needs an **owner** and a **due date**, or it will sit in a report forever.

blocks.title: Linting a draft finding (real run, Python 3)

scenes.caption: Six fields are required. The draft has a title, an impact and evidence, but no fix, owner or due date.
The loop records each missing required field: fix, owner and due.
'XSS vulnerability' has two words: too short to say what is wrong and where.
The impact uses 'may' and 'various', words that commit to nothing. Sorting keeps the output stable between runs.
The rewritten finding passes: a specific title, a concrete impact, evidence, a fix, an owner and a date. A linter cannot judge truth; it only catches missing parts.
scenes.output:
['missing fix', 'missing owner', 'missing due', 'title too short to say what and where', 'vague impact: may', 'vague impact: various']
['ok']

## F-07  Stored XSS in support-ticket subject runs in agents' sessions
Severity: High (client scale, agreed in kickoff)     Confidence: Confirmed
Affected: support.example.com /tickets/view, all agent accounts
Impact:   Any customer who opens a ticket can make script run in the
          browser of the support agent who reads it. The agent's session
          can view and edit every customer's account (about 48,000).
Evidence: 2026-11-10 14:22 UTC, test customer acct cust-test-03.
          Subject set to a harmless marker element; the agent view
          rendered it as markup, not text (screenshot E-07a, redacted).
Fix:      1. Today: none needed beyond the fix; no sign of abuse in logs.
          2. Encode the subject with the template's HTML escaping on output.
          3. Add a strict Content Security Policy to the agent console.
Owner:    Support Portal team (lead: J. Okafor)   Due: 2026-12-04

blocks.caption: An illustrative finding (invented system and people). The evidence proves the bug with a harmless marker instead of a working attack, which keeps the report safe to circulate.

blocks.md: Do not paste working attack strings into client reports "for reproduction". The client needs to confirm the defect and the fix, which a harmless marker or a version check does. Exam reports are different: the exam guide for OSCP+ (OffSec Certified Professional Plus, a hands-on penetration testing certification) requires every step, command and console output so a technically competent reader can replicate the attack. Know which audience you are writing for.

blocks.question: Which finding title is most useful in a ticket list read by an engineering manager?
options: Critical vulnerability found during testing
Burp Suite scanner result #44
CVE-style issue in API
Missing ownership check on /api/invoices/{id} exposes all customers' invoices
blocks.explain: It names the weakness, the location and the consequence, so the manager can route it and judge urgency without opening it. The others say nothing about what or where.

blocks.question: A finding's fix says "Implement proper input validation." What is the main problem?
options: It is too long
It is not specific: it does not say what to change, where, or how the change stops this bug (and validation alone may be the wrong control)
Fixes should never be included in findings
It should name a vendor product
blocks.explain: A useful fix names the exact change and the reason it works: for XSS, context-aware output encoding, with CSP as defence in depth. 'Input validation' is vague and often not the right fix for an output-encoding bug.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite exercise. Draft: "Title: Weak passwords. Impact: Attackers could compromise accounts. Evidence: we cracked some. Fix: enforce a strong password policy." Rewrite the title and impact, and say what evidence you would include.
blocks.reveal:
Title: "Domain password hashes crack offline; 312 of 2,100 cracked in 4 hours, including 3 admins" (numbers from your own test, stated with the method).

Impact: "Anyone who obtains the password hash database (for example after compromising one server) can recover a large share of passwords, including three domain admins, giving control of every computer in the Active Directory domain."

Evidence: how the hashes were obtained under the rules of engagement, tool and wordlist type, counts by account type, cracking time, redacted examples (first and last letters only), never cleartext. Fix: a breached-password deny-list, longer minimums, MFA for admins, and resets for cracked accounts.

lessons.title: Severity you can defend: scores, context and confidence

blocks.md:
Every finding carries a **severity**, and severity is where most arguments with readers start. A severity you cannot explain will be negotiated down; one you can explain gets fixed. Three things make it defensible: say which scale you used, adjust for this environment, and say how sure you are.

Tiny example. NVD (the US National Vulnerability Database) lists the Struts flaw CVE-2017-5638 at **9.8 Critical** under CVSS version 3.1 and at **10.0** under the older CVSS version 2. Same bug, two numbers. A report that says only "CVSS 10" is ambiguous before anyone reads further.

CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System, maintained by FIRST, the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) has metric groups you met in security-basics. The version 4.0 specification is explicit about writing:

- **Base** metrics describe the vulnerability's intrinsic characteristics and assume "the reasonable worst-case impact across different deployed environments".
- **Threat** metrics adjust for things like proof-of-concept code or active exploitation. **Environmental** metrics adjust for your mitigations and how critical the system is.
- Threat and Environmental values are the consumer's job. Vendors and NVD "typically provide only the Base Scores".
- Scores must be labelled with what produced them: **CVSS-B** (base only), **CVSS-BT**, **CVSS-BE** or **CVSS-BTE**. The specification says this nomenclature "should be used wherever a numerical CVSS value is displayed or communicated".

blocks.title: From a public base score to your priority

scenes.caption: The vendor or NVD publishes a base score: the reasonable worst case anywhere. For CVE-2017-5638 NVD gives 9.8 under CVSS 3.1.
Threat information comes next: is there public exploit code, is it exploited now? For Struts in March 2017, yes on both, which pushes urgency up.
Your environment: is the component reachable from the internet, what data sits behind it, what mitigations exist? An internal lab copy and the public dispute portal deserve different priorities.
Confidence is separate from severity: did you confirm the flaw, or only match a version number? Say which. A critical but unconfirmed finding asks for a quick check first.
The finding states all of it in one line: scale and label, the adjustments and why, and the confidence. A reader can now disagree with a specific input instead of with you.

blocks.md:
**Confidence** tells the reader how you know. Three levels cover most findings:

- **Confirmed**: you observed the effect (the server returned another user's record).
- **Likely**: strong indirect evidence (the version is listed as affected and the vulnerable feature is enabled), but you did not trigger it.
- **Possible**: a weak signal (a banner says an old version, but vendors often backport fixes without changing banners).

Many teams also agree a severity scale in the kickoff (for example Critical, High, Medium, Low with written definitions) and use CVSS only as an input. Either is fine if the report states which and applies it consistently. Severity inflation, calling everything critical, teaches readers to ignore your labels.

blocks.code:
Severity: Critical
  Scale:      CVSS-BT 4.0 vector in Appendix B, adjusted per client scale
  Why:        unauthenticated, internet-facing, exploitation seen in the
              wild (CISA KEV), server holds customer dispute files
  Lowered by: nothing found; no WAF rule matched the test request
Confidence: Likely - installed build is in the vendor's affected list;
            vulnerable path reachable; no exploit attempted (ROE 5.2)
blocks.caption: An illustrative severity block. KEV is CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue; ROE are the rules of engagement. WAF is a web application firewall. Each line gives the reader something specific to check or dispute.

blocks.question: A report says only: "Severity: 9.8". What is the most important thing missing?
options: Which scale and version produced it (for example CVSS 3.1 base) and whether it was adjusted for this environment
Nothing; 9.8 is clear
The colour of the severity badge
The name of the tester
blocks.explain: The CVSS 4.0 specification asks for nomenclature (CVSS-B, BT, BE, BTE) wherever a number appears, because the same bug scores differently by version and by which metric groups were used.

blocks.question: You see an old version banner on a Linux server but did not test the flaw. The vendor is known to backport fixes. How should the finding read?
options: Critical, Confirmed
Omit it entirely
Severity per the scale, Confidence: Possible, with a safe check the owner can run (package changelog or vendor advisory) to confirm or close it
Mark it fixed
blocks.explain: A banner is weak evidence when fixes are backported. Stating low confidence and the check that would settle it is honest and saves the owner time.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite exercise. "SEVERITY: CRITICAL!!! This is extremely dangerous and must be fixed immediately." Rewrite the severity line so a sceptical engineer would accept it.
blocks.reveal:
For example: "Severity: High on the client scale (CVSS 3.1 base score 8.1, vector in Appendix B). Kept at High rather than lowered because the endpoint is internet-facing and holds payment data; not Critical because exploitation needs a valid customer account. Confidence: Confirmed (test account cust-test-03, 2026-11-10 14:22 UTC)."

Capitals and adjectives were replaced by a scale, a vector, the reasons for adjusting it, the reason it is not higher, and the evidence behind the confidence.

lessons.title: Whole reports: pentest and audit, read by different people

blocks.md:
A report is a set of documents bound together for different readers. PTES (the Penetration Testing Execution Standard), which you met in pentest-methodology-recon, splits a test report into an **executive summary** for people who own risk and budget and a **technical report** for people who fix things. An **audit report** (an internal or external check of controls against a policy or standard) has the same split, with one extra job: it records management's committed actions and dates.

Tiny example: one report, three readers. The CIO reads two pages and decides funding. The application team reads only their five findings. Next year's auditor reads the appendix to see what was promised and whether it happened.

blocks.title: One report, three readers, three parts

scenes.caption: The report has three layers: summary, findings, and appendices (method, scope, activity log, raw evidence).
Executives read the summary: overall posture, top risks in business terms, the decisions and money needed. They rarely open a finding.
Engineers jump straight to their own findings. Each finding must stand alone: no 'as described above'.
Auditors and retesters use the appendices: what was in scope, what was tested, what management committed to and by when.

blocks.md:
Order matters. Sort findings by severity, then group related ones under the **systemic** cause PTES describes (recall: "lacking effective patch management" versus "MS08-067 missing on one host"). Three missing-patch findings on three servers are one systemic finding with three instances; written that way, the reader sees a process to fix, not three chores.

A helpful shape for a systemic or audit finding has four parts:

- **Condition**: what you found ("12 of 40 internet-facing hosts were more than 90 days behind on critical patches").
- **Criteria**: what it should be, and where that rule comes from (the patch policy, a standard clause).
- **Cause**: why the gap exists ("no owner is assigned per host; patching relies on an email list").
- **Effect**: what it risks or has cost.

Cause is the part most reports skip, and the part that decides whether the fix lasts.

**Case: Equifax's 2015 patch audit.** The House report reproduces an internal Equifax audit from 2015 with eight findings, each paired with a management action and a completion date. Among them: vulnerabilities and systems were not patched in a timely manner; there was no comprehensive IT asset inventory (action due 30 June 2017); and patching ran on an "honor system" with no exception tracker to escalate critical vulnerabilities that missed their deadline.

The report says Equifax did not remediate many of these before the 2017 breach, and in August 2017 a security employee listed six concerns about the ACIS environment, three of which the 2015 audit had already identified. The audit was well written in one sense: clear conditions, actions and dates. What it lacked was a mechanism to make a missed date visible to someone who would act. A report's job does not end at delivery; its findings must land in a tracker with owners, and overdue items must surface.

blocks.code:
1  Executive summary              (2 pages: posture, top 3 risks, decisions)
2  Scope, method and limits        (what was and was not tested, dates, ROE)
3  Findings summary table          (ID, title, severity, confidence, owner, due)
4  Systemic findings               (condition, criteria, cause, effect)
5  Individual findings             (one per issue, each self-contained)
6  Strategic roadmap               (today / this quarter / this year)
A  Activity log                    (UTC, source IP, target, action)
B  Evidence index and CVSS vectors (redacted)
C  Retest results                  (status per finding, date, method)
blocks.caption: An illustrative outline that follows PTES's two audiences. Section 2 includes limits: what you could not test is part of the truth of the report.

blocks.md: State your limits. "We did not test the mobile app; the payment API was out of scope; two days of testing were lost to VPN problems" protects the reader from reading "no findings" as "no problems".

blocks.question: Three findings say "Server A missing patch", "Server B missing patch", "Server C missing patch". What is the better way to write them?
options: Delete two of them as duplicates
Move them to the appendix
Raise all three to Critical so they get attention
One systemic finding about the patch process (condition, criteria, cause, effect) with the three servers as instances
blocks.explain: PTES distinguishes systemic from symptomatic issues. Grouping shows the cause (for example no owner per host) and fixing the cause prevents the next ten instances.

blocks.question: What does the Equifax 2015 audit case show about audit writing?
options: Audits should not include dates
Clear findings with management actions and dates are not enough on their own: something must track them and escalate missed dates
Audits are only for compliance and have no security value
The audit missed the patching problem
blocks.explain: The audit named the patching and inventory problems with actions and dates. Many were not done by the 2017 breach. The weak link was follow-through, which a report must plan for.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite exercise. A report's "Scope" section reads: "Testing was performed on the in-scope systems." Rewrite it so the reader cannot misunderstand what the test covered.
blocks.reveal:
For example: "Scope: the customer web app (app.example.com) and its public API (api.example.com/v2), tested 3 to 14 November 2026 from 198.51.100.40, grey box with two customer test accounts. Out of scope: the mobile apps, the payment provider's hosted pages, internal networks and social engineering. Limits: no source code access; the admin console was unavailable on 6 and 7 November, so admin functions received about one day of testing."

Now a reader knows what "no critical findings" covers, and what it does not.

lessons.title: Executive summaries: one page for the person who decides

blocks.md:
An **executive summary** is the part of a report written for the person who decides: a CIO (chief information officer), a product head, a risk committee. They read it in a few minutes and may never read anything else. It must stand alone.

Tiny example. Weak opening: "Between 3 and 14 November the team performed a grey-box assessment using industry-standard tools and methodologies." Strong opening: "An attacker with a free customer account can read every other customer's invoices. We recommend fixing this before the 1 December launch; it is a two-day change." The first describes your work; the second gives the decision-maker what they need first.

A dependable order for one page:

1. **The answer**: the overall posture in one or two sentences, in business terms.
2. **What matters most**: the top two or three risks, each as a consequence for the business ("customer invoices exposed", "payroll can be changed"), not a bug class.
3. **What we recommend and what it costs**: actions, rough effort, and who must decide.
4. **Trend or comparison** if there is a baseline (last year's test, the previous quarter).
5. **What was not covered**, in one line.

Leave out tool names, CVE numbers, payloads and anything the reader cannot act on. Keep numbers: counts by severity, how many were fixed during the test, how many customers are exposed.

blocks.title: Building a summary top-down: answer, reasons, evidence

scenes.caption: Start with the answer the reader asked for: are we safe to launch, and what must change first?
Support it with a few reasons, each a business consequence. Three is usually enough; more becomes a list nobody remembers.
Each reason points to findings in the technical report. The executive does not need them, but someone checking the summary does.
End with the ask: a decision, an owner and a date. A summary without an ask is a status report.

blocks.code:
BEFORE
  This report presents the results of the security assessment conducted
  by the team. A total of 23 vulnerabilities were identified across
  various severity levels using industry-standard methodologies.
  Remediation is recommended in accordance with best practices.

AFTER
  The new billing portal is not ready to launch. Any customer can read
  every other customer's invoices (about 48,000 accounts) by changing a
  number in the address bar. The fix is a two-day change in one service.

  Other results: 2 high and 6 medium issues, none blocking launch; 15 of
  last year's 18 findings are fixed. Admin accounts without MFA (12 of
  40) remain the largest risk to the wider company.

  Decision needed by 20 Nov (Head of Product): delay launch to 4 Dec,
  or launch with invoice downloads switched off until the fix ships.
blocks.caption: Illustrative, with invented numbers. The 'after' version gives a verdict, the top consequence, the cost of the fix, a trend, and a decision with an owner, options and a date.

blocks.md: Do not soften the verdict to keep a client happy, and do not dramatise it to be noticed. Both destroy the summary's main asset: that the reader can take it at face value. If the news is good, say so plainly; a calibrated "the defences held" is as useful as a warning.

blocks.question: Which sentence belongs in an executive summary?
options: An attacker on the internet can take control of the main firewall; the vendor fix takes about an hour to apply and should be applied today.
We used Nmap 7.95 and Burp Suite to enumerate the attack surface.
CVE-2024-3400 was observed on the edge firewall.
The team worked hard over two weeks.
blocks.explain: It states the consequence in business terms, the cost of fixing it and the urgency. Tool names, bare CVE numbers and effort statements belong elsewhere or nowhere.

blocks.question: A summary lists 23 findings by severity and stops. What is it missing most?
options: A longer methodology section
Screenshots
A verdict and an ask: what the numbers mean for the decision at hand, and what the reader must decide, by when
The CVSS vectors
blocks.explain: Counts without a conclusion leave the decision-maker to do the analysis. The summary's job is to answer their question and state the decision needed.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite exercise. "Overall the security posture is moderate with some areas for improvement. Several high-risk issues were found which should be addressed." Rewrite it as the first two sentences of a summary for a CIO deciding next quarter's budget.
blocks.reveal:
For example: "Our internet-facing systems are well patched, but three ways in remain that would each give an attacker access to customer data. Two can be fixed by the teams this month at no cost; the third (moving 40 admin accounts to phishing-resistant MFA) needs about 30 security keys and a week of help-desk time, which we ask you to fund in Q1."

The rewrite replaces "moderate" with a specific picture, ties risks to consequences, separates free fixes from ones that need money, and makes a concrete budget ask.

lessons.title: Risk memos and exceptions: making someone own the decision

blocks.md:
Not every finding gets fixed on time. Sometimes the fix is expensive, risky or blocked by a vendor. That is allowed, but it must be a **decision** made by someone with the authority to make it, written down, and revisited. Two documents carry it:

- A **risk memo**: a short document that explains a risk and asks a named person to choose a response.
- A **security exception** (also called a risk acceptance or waiver): a time-limited record that a specific system may stay out of policy, with compensating controls and an expiry date.

Tiny example. "We can't patch the dispute portal until the vendor certifies Java 17" is a reason. "The VP of Consumer Apps accepts the residual risk until 30 March; a web application firewall rule and daily log review are in place; the exception expires and comes back to them on that date" is a decision.

Recall from threat-modeling-principles that each risk ends with a response: mitigate, eliminate (avoid), transfer or accept. NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1 (*Integrating Cybersecurity and Enterprise Risk Management*, December 2025, replacing the 2020 edition) gives the vocabulary that makes the memo land with management:

- **Risk appetite**: the broad amount of risk an organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its mission, set by senior leadership.
- **Risk tolerance**: the acceptable variation around that, usually set per programme or system.
- **Accept**: keep a risk that is within tolerance; "no additional risk response action is needed except for monitoring".
- **Risk owner**: "the designated party responsible and accountable" for the risk. It is a person or role, not "IT".

The security team advises; the risk owner decides. Your memo should make that decision easy to make and impossible to make by accident.

blocks.code:
RISK MEMO  RM-2026-031                         Decision needed by: 20 Nov
To:     VP Consumer Apps (risk owner for the dispute portal)
From:   Application Security

Risk    If an attacker exploits the unpatched framework flaw in the
        dispute portal, then they can read uploaded dispute documents
        (about 2.1 million files with ID scans).
Why now Exploitation is public (CISA KEV); the vendor fix needs Java 17,
        which the portal cannot run until its March upgrade.

Options
  A. Patch now with an emergency Java upgrade: 3 weeks, 2 engineers,
     some outage risk.                        Residual risk: low
  B. Accept until 30 Mar with compensating controls (WAF rule for the
     known attack pattern, file access alerts, daily log review).
                                              Residual risk: medium
  C. Take the upload feature offline until March.  Residual risk: low,
     customer impact: disputes by post only.

Recommendation: B, if the controls are live by 22 Nov; otherwise A.
Decision: ______   Signed: ______   Expires: 30 Mar 2027 (returns to owner)
blocks.caption: An illustrative memo (invented numbers). The risk uses the cause-and-effect 'if this happens, then that follows' form of NIST IR 8286 Rev. 1, the options have costs, and the decision line has a signature and an expiry.

blocks.md: Exceptions rot when nobody looks at them. Equifax's 2015 audit named exactly this gap: an "honor system" for patching and no patching exception tracker to escalate critical vulnerabilities that missed their deadline. A tracker can be as simple as a list with four columns that matter: **risk owner**, **compensating control**, **expiry** and **status**, checked automatically. The script below flags exceptions that need a person's attention.

blocks.title: Checking an exception register (real run, Python 3)
blocks.code:
from datetime import date

today = date(2026, 11, 13)
exceptions = [
    # id, system, risk owner, compensating control, expires
    ("EX-12", "dispute-portal", "VP Consumer Apps", "WAF rule, daily log review", date(2026, 9, 30)),
    ("EX-15", "hr-file-share", "", "none", date(2027, 1, 31)),
    ("EX-19", "payments-batch", "Head of Payments", "network isolation", date(2026, 12, 15)),
    ("EX-21", "build-server", "Platform lead", "no inbound access", date(2027, 4, 1)),
]
for ex_id, system, owner, control, expires in exceptions:
    issues = []
    if not owner:
        issues.append("no named risk owner")
    if control == "none":
        issues.append("no compensating control")
    days = (expires - today).days
    if days < 0:
        issues.append(f"expired {-days} days ago")
    elif days <= 45:
        issues.append(f"expires in {days} days: renew or fix")
    print(f"{ex_id} {system:<15} {'; '.join(issues) or 'ok'}")

scenes.caption: Four exceptions, each with an owner, a compensating control and an expiry date. Today is fixed at 13 November 2026 so the output is reproducible.
EX-12 expired on 30 September: 44 days ago. An expired exception is a system out of policy with nobody's decision behind it.
EX-15 has no named risk owner and no compensating control. It is not an exception, just an unfixed problem with paperwork.
scenes.output: EX-15 hr-file-share   no named risk owner; no compensating control

scenes.caption: EX-19 expires in 32 days: time to ask the owner to renew with fresh reasons, or fix. EX-21 is fine.
scenes.output:
EX-12 dispute-portal  expired 44 days ago
EX-15 hr-file-share   no named risk owner; no compensating control
EX-19 payments-batch  expires in 32 days: renew or fix
EX-21 build-server    ok

blocks.md: An exception is a decision with a name, a reason, compensating controls and an end date. Without all four it is just an unfixed vulnerability that someone has stopped looking at.

blocks.question: Who should sign a risk acceptance for an unpatched customer-facing system?
options: The security engineer who found it
Whoever is on call that week
Nobody; acceptances should be verbal
The designated risk owner, who is accountable for the business outcome and has authority to accept it
blocks.explain: NIST IR 8286 defines the risk owner as the party responsible and accountable. Security advises and records; the owner decides. A security engineer accepting business risk is deciding something they do not own.

blocks.question: Why should every exception have an expiry date?
options: So that it is automatically deleted
Because the conditions that justified it (no fix, compensating controls, threat level) change, so the decision must come back to the owner to be made again
Expiry dates are only required by PCI DSS
To make the register shorter
blocks.explain: Threats and fixes change. An expiry forces a fresh decision with current facts, which is exactly what Equifax's 'honor system' lacked.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite exercise. An engineer writes in a ticket: "Can't patch this, it'll break stuff. Closing as won't fix." Rewrite it as a short exception request.
blocks.reveal:
For example: "Exception request for billing-api-02 (CVE-2026-XXXX, High). The vendor patch breaks the invoice export (test run 12 Nov, ticket OPS-881); the vendor promises a fixed build by 15 January. Compensating controls: the service is only reachable from the internal load balancer, and we added an alert on requests to the affected endpoint. Requested expiry: 31 January 2027. Risk owner for approval: Head of Billing. If the vendor build slips, we will take the export offline instead."

The rewrite turns a closure into a decision request: what, why, what reduces the risk meanwhile, until when, and who decides.

lessons.title: Incident updates when you do not know yet

blocks.md:
During an incident, people need information before anyone has the answers. Executives must decide whether to notify customers; engineers must know what to change; support must know what to say. The writer's job is to be useful without overstating what is known.

Tiny example. Hour two of an incident:

- Bad: "We have identified the root cause and the situation is under control." (Is it? If this turns out false, every later update is doubted.)
- Better: "Confirmed: an attacker used one stolen VPN account at 02:14 UTC. Not yet known: whether they reached the customer database; we expect to know by 16:00. Doing now: account disabled, VPN logs being reviewed. Next update: 14:00 UTC, or sooner if this changes."

That structure has four parts and they work for every audience: **confirmed**, **not yet known (and when you expect to know)**, **what we are doing**, and **when the next update comes**. The fixed next-update time matters more than it looks: it stops people interrupting the responders to ask.

Google's book *Site Reliability Engineering* describes incident roles including a communications lead, "the public face of the incident response task force", whose duties include periodic updates to the team and stakeholders. It also asks the incident commander to keep a **living incident document** with the most important information at the top. In security incidents the same role exists, and legal and regulatory notification deadlines add clocks of their own. This lesson is the sentence-level craft. Also mark how far each update may travel: many teams use the Traffic Light Protocol (TLP, from FIRST), whose labels TLP:RED, TLP:AMBER, TLP:GREEN and TLP:CLEAR say who the reader may share it with.

**Words of estimative probability.** Sherman Kent, a member of the CIA's Board of National Estimates, wrote an essay with that title (the CIA declassified it in 1993). In March 1951 a US National Intelligence Estimate said a Soviet attack on Yugoslavia "should be considered a serious possibility". When a policy official asked what odds that meant, Kent said about 65 to 35 in favour; the official had read it as much lower. Kent then asked the board members who had agreed the wording: the lowest had meant odds of about 20 to 80 (a 20% chance), the highest 80 to 20.

Kent proposed tying a few words to number ranges. Kent's chart: **almost certain** (93%, give or take about 6), **probable** (75%, give or take about 12), **chances about even** (50%, give or take about 10), **probably not** (30%, give or take about 10), **almost certainly not** (7%, give or take about 5). Agree such a table in your incident plan, and use the number when no word fits.

blocks.title: Kent's estimative words, and one phrase read three ways

scenes.caption: Kent's five middle words with the probabilities Kent attached to them (centres of each band).
Upper edges (centre plus spread). 'Almost certainly not' ends at 12% but 'probably not' starts at 20%, and 'about even' ends at 60% but 'probable' starts at 63%: no word covers those gaps.
'Serious possibility', 1951: the lowest reader on Kent's board meant about 20%, Kent meant 65%, the highest meant 80%. One phrase, a 60-point spread.

blocks.caption: A small helper using Kent's bands (real run below). 15% and 61% fall between bands, so the honest output is the number.

blocks.code:
90%: 'almost certain' (87-99%)
65%: 'probable' (63-87%)
35%: 'probably not' (20-40%)
15%: no band fits, state the number
61%: no band fits, state the number
blocks.caption: Real output.

blocks.code:
INCIDENT 2026-114  Update 3   13 Nov 14:00 UTC   Next update: 16:00 UTC
Status: contained (attacker access removed); investigation ongoing

Confirmed
  - One VPN account (contractor) used from an unknown host, 02:14-06:40 UTC
  - That session reached file server FS-03; account disabled 06:52
Assessment
  - Customer data accessed: probably not (about 30%). FS-03 holds
    internal documents; no connection to the customer database seen
    in the logs reviewed so far (about 60% of them).
Not yet known
  - How the password was obtained. Expected by: 16:00
Doing now
  - Reviewing remaining logs; resetting the contractor team's passwords
Changes since update 2
  - Session end time moved from 05:10 to 06:40 after VPN log review.
blocks.caption: An illustrative update. It separates fact from judgement, gives the judgement a word and a number, says what evidence it rests on, and lists what changed since the last update.

blocks.md: Never let an update outrun the evidence to sound reassuring. A confident claim that later proves wrong costs more trust than an honest "not yet known". The next lesson is a real case.

blocks.question: Which incident update sentence best states uncertainty?
options: We judge it unlikely (about 30%) that customer data was accessed; this rests on 60% of logs reviewed, and we expect a firmer answer by 16:00.
The attacker definitely did not reach customer data.
Customer data may have potentially been impacted in some way.
We cannot comment during an investigation.
blocks.explain: It gives a word with a number, the basis for the judgement, and when it will improve. 'Definitely did not' overstates, 'may have potentially' is vague, and 'cannot comment' gives readers nothing to plan with.

blocks.question: Why give a fixed time for the next update, even if nothing has changed?
options: Because regulators require it every hour
It makes the incident shorter
It sets expectations, stops people interrupting responders for news, and makes 'no change' itself informative
So the update can be automated
blocks.explain: Predictable updates reduce ad hoc questions and let stakeholders plan. Saying 'no change, next update 16:00' is still useful information.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite exercise. Hour one update: "We are aware of an issue and are investigating. More info soon." Rewrite it with the four-part structure, inventing plausible details.
blocks.reveal:
For example: "13 Nov 09:20 UTC, update 1. Confirmed: since 08:05 UTC our login page has rejected about 40% of valid sign-ins; customers see 'session expired'. Not yet known: whether this is an attack or a faulty deployment; we expect to know by 10:00. Doing now: rolling back this morning's identity service release and checking for unusual sign-in sources. Next update: 10:00 UTC."

Even with little known, the reader learns scope, symptom, the two hypotheses, the action and when to look again.

lessons.title: Case: Storm-0558, a corrected blog and the CSRB report

blocks.md:
In May and June 2023 a threat actor Microsoft calls **Storm-0558** (Storm plus four digits: its temporary label for a developing group; now renamed Antique Typhoon), assessed to be linked to the People's Republic of China, read email in Microsoft Exchange Online (cloud email). The **Cyber Safety Review Board** (CSRB), a US public-private board formed in 2022 to review major cyber incidents (DHS removed its members in January 2025), published its review on 20 March 2024. It found the actor had accessed mailboxes of 22 organisations and 503 related users, including the US Commerce Secretary, and downloaded about 60,000 emails from the State Department alone.

The attacker used authentication tokens signed with a Microsoft consumer signing key (an MSA key, Microsoft Services Account) created in 2016, which a separate validation flaw let work on enterprise mail. The State Department noticed first, on 15 and 16 June, through a custom alert it had built (nicknamed "Big Yellow Taxi") on an audit log called MailItemsAccessed, which it could see because it paid for a premium logging licence.

This case is in a writing course because of what happened next. On 6 September 2023 Microsoft published a blog post, "Results of Major Technical Investigations for Storm-0558 Key Acquisition". It said a 2021 crash of a signing system had produced a crash dump (a snapshot of a crashed process's memory) that "incorrectly contained the key", that the dump was moved to a corporate debugging environment, and that an engineer's account compromised by the actor could reach it. It called this "the most probable mechanism".

The CSRB reports that soon afterwards Microsoft found no crash dump containing the key. Microsoft told the Board in November 2023 that the post was inaccurate, and told it the errors were "not material". The post was not corrected until an addendum on 12 March 2024, after repeated questions from the Board. The CSRB's reasoning: customers relied on the post to judge whether the way in had been closed; a key lost "through unknown means is far more significant" than one lost through a known and fixed path.

blocks.title: Storm-0558: the intrusion and the public statements (2023 to 2024)

scenes.caption: May to June 2023: the actor reads mailboxes. Mid-June: State's alert fires and it contacts Microsoft.
July 2023: Microsoft's first two posts (11 and 14 July) disclose forged tokens and give indicators and technical detail.
6 September: a post names the crash dump as the most probable mechanism. Soon after, Microsoft finds no dump containing the key.
November 2023 to March 2024: Microsoft has told the Board the post is inaccurate, but the public text stays unchanged for more than six months.
12 March 2024: addendum published. 20 March: the CSRB report, which lists the late correction among its reasons for calling Microsoft's security culture inadequate.

blocks.code:
AS PUBLISHED (6 Sep 2023, quoted in the CSRB report)
  "...this was the most probable mechanism by which the actor
   acquired the key."

A CALIBRATED VERSION (illustrative)
  Leading hypothesis: key material left the signing environment in a
  2021 crash dump and was reached through a compromised engineer
  account. Status: not confirmed. We have not found a crash dump
  containing this key, and we have no logs showing how it was taken.
  We are testing other hypotheses. We will update this post when the
  evidence changes; last reviewed 6 Sep 2023.
blocks.caption: The calibrated version is illustrative, not Microsoft's text. It separates hypothesis from evidence, states what is missing, and promises an update. The CSRB notes Microsoft developed 46 hypotheses in total.

blocks.md:
**The CSRB report as a model of institutional writing.** Read its structure, not just its findings:

- **Facts are separated from judgements.** Section 1 (Facts: overview, intrusion details, incident management, public reporting) comes before Section 2 (Findings and Recommendations), so a reader can check the evidence before meeting the conclusions.
- **Conclusions come first and are numbered.** The executive summary states that the intrusion "was preventable and should never have occurred" and that Microsoft's security culture "was inadequate", then lists seven numbered reasons.
- **Counterfactuals make causes concrete.** "If Microsoft had not paused manual rotation of keys..." sentences show which single change would have stopped or narrowed the attack.
- **Recommendations are numbered, addressed and testable.** There are 25, each naming who should act (Microsoft, all cloud providers, CISA, NIST). Recommendation 5, for example, sets log retention for identity systems of at least two years beyond a key's expiry.

When an earlier statement turns out wrong, correct it publicly, quickly and visibly, and say what changed. Readers make decisions on what you wrote; leaving an error standing keeps those decisions wrong.

blocks.question: Why did the CSRB treat an inaccurate root-cause blog as a serious problem rather than a communications slip?
options: Because blogs are legally binding
Because the blog named the wrong threat actor
Because it was published too quickly
Because customers used it to assess their own risk; believing the cause was known and closed, they lacked essential facts while the real cause was still unknown
blocks.explain: The Board wrote that customers relied on the public statements, and that a key lost through unknown means is far more significant than one lost through a known path, since nobody can say the hole is closed.

blocks.question: What structural choice in the CSRB report helps a sceptical reader most?
options: Using no numbers
Separating a facts section from the findings and recommendations, and numbering both reasons and recommendations
Putting the recommendations before the facts
Avoiding any footnotes
blocks.explain: Separating evidence from judgement lets readers test the conclusions; numbering lets later readers track which recommendations were adopted.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite exercise. A status page says: "Root cause identified: a misconfigured firewall rule. The issue is fully resolved." Two days later you learn the rule change was a symptom of a stolen admin token, and you do not yet know how the token was stolen. Write the correction.
blocks.reveal:
For example: "Update 15 Nov, correcting our 13 Nov statement. We said the root cause was a misconfigured firewall rule. That was wrong: the rule was changed by an attacker using a stolen administrator token. The token has been revoked and all admin sessions reset. We do not yet know how the token was stolen; our leading hypothesis is a compromised laptop, which we are examining. If you rely on our admin API, review your audit log for changes between 10 and 13 Nov. Next update by 18 Nov."

It names the old claim, says plainly it was wrong, gives the new facts and the remaining unknowns, tells readers what to do, and commits to a next update.

lessons.title: Design-review and code-review comments that get acted on

blocks.md:
A **design review** is a check of a proposed system before it is built (often a written design document); a **code review** checks a change before it merges (on GitHub a pull request, PR; at Google a changelist, CL). Security engineers write many short comments in both. Each one competes with dozens of others for the author's attention, so it must say how much it matters and why.

Tiny example, same concern twice:

- "This is insecure."
- "issue (security, blocking): The upload handler trusts the client's Content-Type, so a user can upload an HTML file that the CDN (content delivery network, the caching servers in front of the site) then serves from our domain. Could we check the file's bytes and serve uploads from a separate domain? Happy to pair on it."

Google publishes its code review guidance (the eng-practices site). For comments it asks reviewers to:

- **Be courteous; comment on the code, never the developer.** Its example rewrites "Why did you use threads here when there's obviously no benefit..." into a statement about the code.
- **Explain why**, so the author learns and can push back with facts.
- **Balance pointing out problems with direct guidance**: sometimes a suggestion or even code is more helpful.
- **Label severity**: "Nit:" (minor), "Optional" or "Consider", "FYI". Without labels, the guide notes, authors may treat every comment as mandatory.

**Conventional Comments** (conventionalcomments.org, "comments that are easy to grok and grep") formalises labels as `label (decorations): subject` with an optional discussion. Labels include praise, nitpick, suggestion, issue, todo, question, thought, chore and note; decorations such as `blocking`, `non-blocking` or `security` add context. Its example: "suggestion (security): I'm a bit concerned that we are implementing our own DOM purifying function here..."

blocks.code:
import re

PATTERN = re.compile(r"^(?P<label>\w+)(?: \((?P<decos>[^)]*)\))?: (?P<subject>.+)$")
comments = [
    "issue (security,blocking): The upload handler trusts the client's Content-Type.",
    "nitpick: Rename tmp to upload_path.",
    "suggestion (security,non-blocking): Log rejected uploads with the user id.",
    "This seems wrong.",
]
for c in comments:
    m = PATTERN.match(c)
    if not m:
        print(f"{'UNLABELLED':<11}{'?':<7}{c}")
        continue
    decos = m["decos"].split(",") if m["decos"] else []
    print(f"{m['label']:<11}{'block' if 'blocking' in decos else '-':<7}{m['subject']}")
blocks.caption: A tiny parser for the Conventional Comments format (real run below). Labelled comments are machine-readable; the unlabelled one tells the author nothing about urgency.

blocks.code:
issue      block  The upload handler trusts the client's Content-Type.
nitpick    -      Rename tmp to upload_path.
suggestion -      Log rejected uploads with the user id.
UNLABELLED ?      This seems wrong.
blocks.caption: Real output.

blocks.title: A security review thread that converges

scenes.caption: The reviewer leads with the blocking issue: what is wrong, the concrete scenario, and a proposed fix.
Non-blocking items are labelled so the author can defer them without guilt.
The author disagrees with facts: the CDN already sets a download header. A good reviewer checks rather than insists.
The reviewer verifies and narrows the ask: the header covers browsers, but the API returns the file inline. One change remains.
The author pushes a fix; the reviewer approves and records the follow-up as a ticket, not a lingering comment.

blocks.md:
A security comment that gets acted on usually has five parts:

1. **Label and blocking status** (is this a merge blocker?).
2. **The defect**, located precisely (file and line, or design section).
3. **The scenario**: who could do what, in one sentence. Without it, the author must imagine the attack themselves.
4. **A suggested fix**, or a question if you are not sure the problem is real (Conventional Comments recommends `question:` for that).
5. **An offer or a pointer**: a link to the internal guideline, a library to use, time to pair.

In design reviews, write at the design's level: "the session service trusts the user id in the JWT (JSON Web Token, a signed token format) from the mobile app without verifying the signature" rather than line-level details, and say which threat (from your STRIDE list, recall threat-modeling-principles) the comment addresses.

blocks.question: Which review comment is most likely to get a correct fix quickly?
options: issue (security, blocking): /export joins a user-supplied path to the reports directory, so ../ can reach other files. Could we resolve it and check it stays inside? Helper: docs/safe-paths.md
Insecure. Fix.
Why would anyone build it like this?
nitpick: path handling
blocks.explain: It is labelled and blocking, locates the defect, gives the scenario, proposes a specific fix and points to a helper. The others give no reason, attack the author, or understate a real issue as a nitpick.

blocks.question: You are not sure a pattern in a PR is exploitable. What is the best comment?
options: Block the merge until the author proves it is safe
Say nothing
A question: explain the concern and ask whether this input can ever come from a user, marked non-blocking unless the answer is yes
Mark it as an issue and Critical to be safe
blocks.explain: Questions are for uncertain concerns. Blocking on a guess burns trust; silence risks missing a bug. A clear question gets the author's knowledge on the record.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite exercise. Rewrite this design review comment: "Storing tokens in localStorage is bad practice. Please follow best practices."
blocks.reveal:
For example: "issue (security, blocking): Section 4.2 stores the refresh token in localStorage, where any script running on our origin can read it. One XSS bug anywhere on app.example.com would then let an attacker keep a user's session for 30 days. Could we keep the refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie scoped to /auth, which page scripts cannot read? Our auth guide covers this pattern; happy to review the revised section."

The rewrite names the location, the mechanism, the consequence with its duration, a specific alternative and why it helps, and an offer.

lessons.title: Getting a fix shipped when you cannot order it

blocks.md:
Security engineers rarely own the systems they find problems in. They cannot order a product team to drop its roadmap. **Influence without authority** means getting the fix shipped anyway, by making it easy, clearly owned, and visible to the people who do have authority.

Tiny example. A security engineer files "SQL injection in reports service" in a shared backlog and waits. Nothing happens for two months. Another opens a ticket assigned to the reports team's lead, links a pull request that already fixes it with a test, offers to review, and asks for a merge date. The fix ships that week. Same bug; different writing and different effort.

What moves fixes, in rough order of strength:

- **A named owner.** Equifax's patch policy named roles but, the House report says, nobody was officially designated for them; the alert went to a list. Find the person: the asset inventory, the code owners file, the on-call rota.
- **A cheap fix.** A ready pull request, a config snippet, a library call. Every hour you remove from the owner's cost raises the odds.
- **A reason in their terms.** Customer data, outage risk, an audit date, a launch. Not "best practice".
- **A date and a follow-up.** Agreed service-level targets (for example 15 days for critical) turn your request into their commitment.
- **A visible, predictable escalation path.** Said up front, not as a threat: "if this misses the date we will review it in the monthly risk meeting with your director." Escalation is a routine part of the process, not a personal failure.

blocks.title: From finding to merged fix, with an escalation that stays polite

scenes.caption: The security engineer opens a ticket assigned to the owning team's lead, with the scenario, a ready PR and a proposed date.
The owner pushes back: the sprint is full. This is normal and is information, not refusal.
The engineer offers options with costs: merge the ready PR (2 hours of review), or request a time-limited exception signed by the risk owner.
No decision by the agreed date, so the pre-announced path is used: the decision goes to the director who owns both the roadmap and the risk.
The director chooses: merge this week. The engineer reviews quickly, then retests and closes with evidence.
