blocks.md:
**Scale it up.** One engineer influences a team; a security programme influences a company the same way: owners, cheap fixes, reasons, dates, routine escalation. The CSRB's first recommendation to Microsoft was aimed at exactly that level: its CEO and Board of Directors should develop and share publicly a plan with specific timelines for security reforms, and hold leaders at all levels accountable for it. Its second suggested deprioritising feature work until substantial security improvements were made. Influence at the top is still writing: a plan with dates that someone senior signs.

**Keep relationships.** Credit teams publicly when they fix things fast, keep your severity honest so your "urgent" stays believable, and never surprise an owner by escalating without having told them the path first.

Escalation is not a weapon. If owners learn that talking to security means being reported upward, they stop talking to security, and you lose the early warnings that matter most. Agree the path in advance, use it predictably, and make the first step always a direct conversation.

blocks.question: A team ignores a High finding for six weeks. What is the most effective next message?
options: A broadcast email to the whole engineering department
Silently lower the severity so the backlog looks better
Fix it yourself in production without telling them
A message to the team lead offering the ready fix or an exception, with a date, and naming the pre-agreed escalation if neither happens
blocks.explain: It makes the cheapest path obvious, gives the owner a real choice including a formal exception, and uses a known escalation route rather than public shaming or unilateral action.

blocks.question: Why did Equifax's emailed patch alert fail as an influence attempt, in this lesson's terms?
options: It was too technical
It had no named owner, no reply or follow-up step, and no routine escalation when nothing happened
It was sent by the wrong team
It did not use CVSS
blocks.explain: The House report found no designated owners and no redundancy to confirm action. Those are exactly the levers this lesson lists: owner, date, follow-up and escalation.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite exercise. Slack message: "Hey, you really need to fix that S3 bucket thing, it's super dangerous." (S3 is Amazon's Simple Storage Service; a bucket is one storage container in it.) Rewrite it as a message to the bucket's owner that is likely to get it fixed today.
blocks.reveal:
For example: "Hi Mei, the bucket acme-exports-prod (owned by Data Platform per the inventory) allows public read, so anyone with the URL list can download yesterday's customer export (about 12,000 rows with emails and addresses). The fix is Block Public Access, which overrides public permissions; I checked that no public consumer uses it (access log, last 30 days). Could you apply it today? I can screen-share if useful. If it needs to stay public for a reason I've missed, let's talk at 15:00 and I'll raise it with your director's risk review."

Owner by name, exact resource, consequence with a number, specific fix, evidence the fix is safe, a time, an offer, and a calm escalation path.

lessons.title: Presenting to a board: risk, money and decisions

blocks.md:
A **board of directors** oversees a company on behalf of its owners. It does not run security; it asks whether management is managing the risk, and it approves big decisions. A security briefing to a board is short, read in advance, and judged on one question: do the directors now understand the main risks well enough to ask good questions and make the decisions in front of them?

Tiny example. Weak slide: "We blocked 4.2 million attacks this quarter." Strong slide: "Our largest risk is ransomware stopping order fulfilment. Today we could restore core systems in about five days; our target is two. Closing that gap needs immutable backups for 14 systems, which is the budget item on today's agenda." The first is a number with no decision; the second is a risk, a measure, a gap and an ask.

In the US, board oversight of cyber risk is now something public companies must describe. The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) adopted rules on 26 July 2023. They add **Item 106** to Regulation S-K (the SEC's rules for the non-financial content of company filings), which requires companies to describe in their annual report (Form 10-K) the board's oversight of risks from cybersecurity threats, any board committee responsible, and how the board is informed about those risks. They also add **Item 1.05** to Form 8-K (the form for reporting major events): a material cybersecurity incident must generally be disclosed within four business days after the company determines it is material.

So your briefing is evidence of oversight. Write it so that a director could later explain what they were told and what they decided.

What directors can use:

- **Few risks, in business language**: three to five top risks, each tied to a business outcome (revenue stopped, data exposed, regulatory penalty) and a trend (better, worse, same).
- **Measures that show control, not activity**: time to fix critical issues, share inside agreed targets, restore time in the last test, coverage of MFA on admin accounts. Avoid counts that only grow with traffic ("attacks blocked").
- **Honest comparison**: against last quarter, against your own targets, or against a recognised framework.
- **Decisions and asks** stated as options with costs.
- **Incidents**: what happened, impact, what changed. No blame, no drama.

blocks.caption: Turning a quarter's closed findings into board measures (real run below). The numbers are invented sample data; the method is the point: median time and share inside the target, per severity.

blocks.code:
critical median  14 days; 3/5 inside the 15-day target (60%)
high     median  33 days; 3/7 inside the 30-day target (43%)
blocks.caption: Real output. A median resists one very slow item better than an average does.

blocks.title: Two ways to show the same quarter to a board

scenes.caption: Activity view: counts that sound impressive but carry no target and no decision. A director cannot tell if this is good.
Control view: share of fixes inside target. Critical 60%, High 43%, both below an 80% goal. Now there is a gap to discuss and a decision to make.

blocks.md: Do not present fear or vanity. Breach headlines from other companies and "millions of attacks blocked" both waste the board's attention. Directors respond to clear risk, honest measures and a specific ask, and they remember who was straight with them.

blocks.question: Which slide title is best for a board?
options: Ransomware could stop order fulfilment for about 5 days; target 2; closing the gap needs the backup budget on today's agenda
Firewall dropped 4.2M packets from 37 countries
We are fully compliant with all frameworks
Top 10 CVEs this quarter
blocks.explain: It names a business outcome, a measured current state, a target and the decision needed. The others are activity, an unfalsifiable claim, or technical detail directors cannot act on.

blocks.question: Under the SEC rules adopted in July 2023, what must a public company describe about the board in its annual report?
options: Each director's password policy
Every vulnerability found during the year
The board's oversight of risks from cybersecurity threats, any responsible committee, and how the board is informed about those risks
Nothing; the rules only cover incidents
blocks.explain: Regulation S-K Item 106(c)(1) requires a description of board oversight, the responsible committee if any, and the processes by which the board is informed. Item 1.05 of Form 8-K separately covers material incidents.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite exercise. Board slide bullet: "Security posture improved significantly in Q3 thanks to many new tools and initiatives." Rewrite it as one or two bullets a director could question and remember.
blocks.reveal:
For example:

- "Admin accounts with phishing-resistant MFA: 22% in Q2, 85% in Q3; the remaining 15% are in the plant control network, planned for Q1."
- "Critical findings fixed inside 15 days: 60% (target 80%). Main cause: two legacy systems with no owner; we ask the board to note the Q1 decommissioning decision."

Each bullet has a measure, a trend or target, a reason and, where needed, an ask. A director can now ask "why only 60%?" and get a concrete answer.

lessons.title: Writing for disclosure: vendor reports, advisories and Project Zero

blocks.md:
**Coordinated vulnerability disclosure** (CVD) is the process of getting a vulnerability from the person who found it to the people who can fix it, and then to the public, so that fixes are deployed. You met disclosure and CVE records in security-basics. Here the focus is the two documents involved: the **report to the vendor** and the **public advisory**.

The CERT Coordination Center (CERT/CC), at Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute, has coordinated disclosures since 1988. Its *Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure* says a report should give: exact affected versions; how the flaw was found; proof-of-concept code or reproduction steps; ideally a suggested fix; the impact and an attack scenario; and time constraints such as a planned talk. Thin reports, it warns, may be delayed or rejected.

**Project Zero as a style model.** Google's Project Zero team publishes its bug reports at its deadline. Its 2026 policy post says the team holds itself "to high standards with regards to the reproducibility, readability, reachability and reported security impact" of its reports. Example: team member Tavis Ormandy's 2017 report on a Cloudflare memory leak, titled "cloudflare: Cloudflare Reverse Proxies are Dumping Uninitialized Memory". Read its shape:

- **Title**: vendor prefix, then the effect in plain words.
- **Context**: what they were doing (a fuzzing corpus project) when odd data appeared.
- **Trigger**: what reproduced it (certain unbalanced HTML tags on pages behind the proxy).
- **Observed impact**: what samples showed (keys, cookies, passwords, POST data from other sites), stated as fact.
- **Action**: they stopped and contacted Cloudflare's security team, via Twitter, because on a Friday evening "seconds mattered".
- **Deadline**: the standard 90-day footer.

Cloudflare's incident report says it disabled the first affected feature 47 minutes after getting details.

**Deadlines are writing decisions too.** Project Zero's policy changes reflect how disclosure timing works:

- Since 2021 it used "90 + 30": up to 90 days to fix, plus 30 days for patches to reach users.
- A July 2025 trial, *Reporting Transparency*, publishes the vendor, product and report date within about a week of reporting, with no technical details.
- On 13 November 2026 it announced a **"Full X"** policy: details are disclosed X days after the report, whether or not a fix exists. X is 90 now, 60 from 2 February 2027 and 30 from 3 January 2028. The post gives the reason: AI-assisted discovery and exploitation have shortened the time attackers need, including the time to reverse-engineer a patch.
- Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild follow Google's 7-day policy, and a vendor can ask for earlier disclosure.

Whatever your own deadline, state it in the first message, so the vendor can plan.

blocks.title: Project Zero disclosure clocks under Full X (days after report)

scenes.caption: Full 90, from 13 November 2026: details become public on day 90, whether the vendor patched on day 47, day 90, or not at all.
From 2 February 2027 the window is 60 days; from 3 January 2028, 30 days. Vendors must fix faster or protect users some other way.
Exploited in the wild: 7 days under Google's policy, because users are already being attacked.
Since July 2025, a short public notice (vendor, product, report date) appears about a week after the report. It is an alert, not a blueprint: no technical details until the deadline.

blocks.md: **Finding the right reader.** RFC 9116 defines **security.txt**, a file at `/.well-known/security.txt` that tells researchers how to report. Two fields are mandatory: `Contact` (an email, phone or web address) and `Expires` (after which the file is stale and should not be used; RFC 9116 recommends less than a year ahead). Check it before you write; a report to a support inbox can sit unread. The checker below catches a common failure: a file whose expiry has passed.

blocks.code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone

text = """# https://example.com/.well-known/security.txt
Contact: mailto:security@example.com
Expires: 2026-01-31T00:00:00Z
Policy: https://example.com/security-policy
"""
fields = {}
for line in text.splitlines():
    if line and not line.startswith("#"):
        name, _, value = line.partition(": ")
        fields.setdefault(name.lower(), []).append(value)

now = datetime(2026, 11, 13, tzinfo=timezone.utc)
print("Contact present:", "contact" in fields)
expires = datetime.fromisoformat(fields["expires"][0].replace("Z", "+00:00"))
print("Expires:", expires.date(), "STALE" if expires < now else "valid")
blocks.caption: Real run, Python 3. Output: 'Contact present: True' then 'Expires: 2026-01-31 STALE'. A stale file means the contact may be wrong; look for another route (a bug bounty page, CERT/CC) rather than giving up.

blocks.md: **The public advisory** is written for the people who must act: administrators and downstream vendors. CERT/CC's guide stresses that the point of disclosure is to provoke action, and that information can be *public* (a commit message, a diff) without being *publicised*. A useful advisory states, near the top: the product and **affected versions**, the **fixed versions**, a **workaround** if patching must wait, the impact in one sentence, the CVE ID, whether exploitation is known, and credit to the finder. Technical depth can follow, but a reader who stops after five lines should know whether they are affected and what to do.

Subject: [Security] Unauthenticated file read in AcmeFiles 4.2.0-4.2.6

Product / versions: AcmeFiles server 4.2.0 to 4.2.6 (4.1.x not affected;
                    tested on 4.2.6, Ubuntu 24.04, default config)
Summary:  An unauthenticated request to /api/preview can read any file the
          service account can read, including the config file holding the
          database password.
How found: code review of the preview handler while testing an integration.
Reproduce: attached script check_preview.py reads only /etc/hostname and
          prints it; please run it against a test instance.
Suggested fix: resolve the path and reject it unless it stays inside the

Timeline: I plan to publish 90 days from today (11 Feb 2027), earlier if

Contact:  PGP key fingerprint ...   Credit as: R. Osei
blocks.caption: An illustrative vendor report following CERT/CC's checklist. The reproduction reads a harmless file, enough to prove the bug without shipping a weapon in an email that may be forwarded. PGP (Pretty Good Privacy) is the usual email encryption for such reports.

blocks.question: A researcher's first email to a vendor says: "Your product has a critical RCE. Contact me for details." What is the main problem?
options: It is too long
RCE must always be disclosed publicly first
Vendors do not accept email
It gives the vendor nothing to triage: no version, no reproduction, no impact scenario, no timeline, so it is likely to be delayed or dismissed
blocks.explain: CERT/CC's checklist (versions, how found, reproduction, fix idea, impact, time constraints) exists because thin reports stall. RCE is remote code execution; saying so without evidence invites doubt.

blocks.question: Under Project Zero's Full 90 policy, a vendor patches on day 47. When are the details published?
options: Day 47
Day 90
Day 77, after 30 days of patch uptake
Never, because it is fixed
blocks.explain: Full X discloses X days after the report regardless of when the fix lands; the policy page's own example is a day-47 patch disclosed on day 90. Earlier only if the vendor asks, or if the bug is exploited in the wild or already public.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite exercise. A public advisory begins with three paragraphs on the history of the affected protocol, and only in paragraph four says which versions are affected. Rewrite the first five lines.
blocks.reveal:
For example:

"AcmeFiles server 4.2.0 to 4.2.6 lets an unauthenticated attacker read files on the server, including stored credentials (CVE-2026-XXXXX, CVSS-B 4.0 vector below). Fixed in 4.2.7, released 11 February 2027. If you cannot upgrade now, block /api/preview at your proxy. We are not aware of exploitation. Thanks to R. Osei for reporting it."

Affected versions, impact, fixed version, workaround, exploitation status and credit come first; the background can follow for those who want it.

blocks.md:
**Practise this course legally.** Writing improves only with practice on real findings you were allowed to make.

- [PortSwigger Web Security Academy](https://portswigger.net/web-security): after each lab, write a full finding (title, impact, evidence, fix) as if for a client.
- [OWASP Juice Shop](https://owasp.org/www-project-juice-shop/): run it locally, then write a two-page report with an executive summary and three findings.
- [TryHackMe](https://tryhackme.com/) and [Hack The Box](https://www.hackthebox.com/): many free rooms; write an exam-style report for one machine, then a client-style version of the same finding and compare them.
- [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/): Carnegie Mellon's free practice; write a short incident update for one challenge as if it were happening to you.

Test only systems you own or have written permission to test. For every piece of writing, ask a friend outside security to read your executive summary and tell you what they would do next; if they cannot, rewrite it.

Disclosure writing is for action: give the vendor everything needed to reproduce and fix, give the public what they need to know if they are affected and what to do, and state your timeline at the start.
